title: The empty basin, which is silent until it is a vowel

slides.heading: One letter, two jobs, and the last corner of a grid
body: The letter from lesson six finally gets its name.
Two jobs, one glyph, and the position tells you which.
A short vowel to go with the long one.
And the last two tone rules the market needs.

slides.heading: Pen and paper
body: Real paper, a real pen.
Both halves of the name, out loud, every time.

slides.heading: The basin
body: Its name is the sound, then a word beginning with that sound.
The word means a **basin**.
A plain open ring. Mid class, in the market.

slides.heading: The woman who sold nothing
body: A pitch is kept only while something of yours is standing in it.
The fish-seller set an empty basin in her sister's place.
She filled it every day for four months so it would look like somebody's.

slides.heading: What the basin was for
body: The pitch was still there in the autumn, because the basin had been.
It sold nothing and held nothing but water.
Standing in a slot, saying nothing, keeping the place open.

slides.heading: The basin's letter
body: A plain ring, standing open.
One stroke, and every part of it curved.

slides.heading: Write it
body: **Start at the head**, upper left, clockwise.
Carry the ring round and close it.
You drew this in lesson six without knowing its name.

slides.heading: Job one, and it is the basin's job
body: A syllable is written consonant first, and Thai keeps to that.
Some words open on a vowel and have no consonant to write.
The basin stands in the slot and makes no sound.

slides.heading: Read this one
body: The ring, silent. Then the roof's lodger, then the chicken stopping it.
Out loud before you turn it over.

slides.heading: That one
body: **อีก** — more, or again.
The ring says nothing. The vowel behind it is the sound.

slides.heading: And this is what the prop was
body: **มือ** — a hand. **คือ** — is.
The prop from lesson six was this letter the whole time.
Front of a word or under a bare vowel, it holds a place and says nothing.

slides.heading: Job two, where the basin fills up
body: Put the ring after a consonant with no vowel written between them.
It stops being silent and becomes a long aw.
The jaw drops all the way, as in the English word *saw*.

slides.heading: Read this one
body: Mouse, basin as the vowel, mouse again closing it.
Hold the vowel long. Out loud before you turn it over.

slides.heading: That one
body: **นอน** — to lie down, or to sleep.
Harbour letter, live ending, flat and level.

slides.heading: Both jobs in one word
body: The first ring: silent, holding the slot.
The second ring: the long vowel.
Then the chicken's letter stopping it. Out loud first.

slides.heading: That one
body: **ออก** — out, or to go out.
The same letter twice: silent, then the vowel.

slides.prompt: Two syllables, each written with the ring. In one it is the first character; in the other it follows a consonant with nothing written between them. Which is silent, and which is the vowel?

answers: At the front: **silent**, holding an empty consonant slot.
Behind a consonant with nothing between: the long **aw**.
The position settles it, without your knowing the word.

slides.heading: And the short version
body: **เ-าะ** — the mast in front, the post behind, the two hooks last.
The same mouth as the long aw, cut off early.
Long and short are two separate vowels here, as they have been since lesson one.

slides.heading: Read this one
body: Three marks of vowel, wrapped round the chicken's letter.
Short. Out loud before you turn it over.

slides.heading: That one
body: **เกาะ** — an island.
Market letter, short vowel, stopped dead.
Read from the page. This one has no recording here.
The tone on it is the thing still missing.

slides.heading: Three corners you already hold
body: A tone comes from the district, and from live against dead.
Four corners per district, and the market has had one since lesson three.
**ตาม** — to follow. Market letter, live ending, flat and level.
The two dead corners are all that is left.

slides.heading: The market's four corners, closed
body: Market letter, dead ending, short vowel: **low**.
Market letter, dead ending, long vowel: **low**.
The length is written into both rules, and both give the same answer.
**เกาะ** is short. **ออก** is long. Both are low.

slides.heading: Why that is a gift, and what the harbour charges instead
body: Harbour, dead, short: **high**. Harbour, dead, long: **falling**.
Market, dead: **low**, at either length.
The harbour makes you measure the vowel. The market takes the letter and stops.

slides.prompt: บอก and เกาะ both open on a market letter and both end dead, one with a long vowel and one with a short one. What tone does each take, and how many rules did you need?

answers: One rule in practice, because both lengths give the same answer.
The market's grid is closed, in all four corners.

slides.heading: Words the basin gives you
body: **ชอบ** — to like. **บอก** — to tell. **ตอบ** — to answer.
**ยอม** — to permit. **พอ** — enough. **รอ** — to wait.
**ตอน** — a part, or a moment. **มอง** — to look at.
**อายุ** — age. **อาชีพ** — an occupation. **อาจ** — may, or might.
**อัน** — the classifier for small things. **อา** — a parent's younger sibling.

slides.heading: Twenty-one letters, and the end of a run
body: Twenty-one letters, twenty vowel spellings.
The market's tone grid is closed, and the harbour's has been since lesson five.
Next: the temple, and the seven letters you were shown the map of.
